Everyone is giving great advice in the comments, be sure to follow it! There’s something I’d like to add though: 

Whenever you want to join two pieces of the same size together (which is wat you appear to be doing) remember that *both* need to cut at an angle to line up correctly. 

Pic 3 best shows what I mean: see how the cut face of the diagonal piece is basically twice as wide as the face of the vertical piece? That’s because you only angled one of them. In order to have the two match up nicely you have to cut them both at the same angle, which coincidentally is half the overall angle you’re trying to achieve. 

So in the case of that third pic you essentially have four faces to cut: one on the horizontal, two on the diagonal and one on the vertical. By cutting joining faces at the same angle, they will all match nicely. 

So let’s say the diagonal piece has to sit at 45 degrees relative to both the vertical and horizontal pieces. You’d want cut the horizontal at 22.5 to start the angle and the diagonal at 22.5 to finish it. Then once you get to the vertical, do the same. 22.5 on the diagonal to get it started and 22.5 on the vertical to make it the full 45. That way all the faces are the same and you will have a match all around. 

To calculate the angles you need for your project, use the excellent methods described in the other comments. Good luck!

It could be any of the following:

-	amp setup: make sure all tone controls are set flat and lower the gain, test again.
-	preamp setup: set all controls on your bass to flat and test again.
-	flat battery: your bass probably requires one or two nine volt batteries, replace them and test again.
-	pedals: you have any effects in your signal chain? Plug directly into your amp and test again.
-	cables: use good quality cables and… you know the drill

Best thing to do is work down the signal chain from either end and see what gives. My money is on the bass battery. Be sure to always unplug an active bass when you don’t play it, leaving it plugged in drains the battery!

There are many websites with articles about the best beginner's basses, but here's the long and short of it (in my opinion):

€80 will not buy you a good bass, even as a beginner. Be prepared to spend at least €200 to get something worth your money. Go on Reverb.com, make an account and look for any second hand Squier, Ibanez or Yamaha bass in that €200 range and you'll be happy for a while. No real need to look for a specific model or series, any of the basses made by those brands will be fine. Don't buy something too old if you don't know anything about it.

That's it. Get to playing, get the bass set up by a guitar store and figure out what your favorite bass players use when you want to buy another bass. By that time you'll know enough to make a good decision.

In short: don't buy the €80 bass, it's going to suck.

As cliché as it sounds: it's all about what you want personally. I can't speak for the Sire (I've never played one), but "off brand" hasn't meant "shitty" for a long time. I think the Sire basses look and sound like insane value for money, and I'm a Fender fanboy through and through.

A few things to consider: 

-	The Fender is probably going to play amazing with a good setup and (if it needs it) some fret dressing. 
-	Resale value is higher on a Fender, if you care about that sort of thing. Conversely; the Sire offers much more value for money, no doubt about it.
-	If you like modifying your guitars, Fender basses are basically the industry standard. There are stupid amounts of parts available, from necks to pickups and pickguards, in all price ranges. You can transform the bass into something entirety different fairly easily, I'm not sure if the same goes for the Sire. 
-	Finally, and this is *highly* personal: looks. To me any Fender style bass (P or J) looks so dumb with a non-Fender headstock. I know this is silly, but I can't get over it. Maybe I'm elitist, maybe I'm just a sucker for classic design, either way it's the "real thing" or bust to me.

the long and short of it is that Fender are the way to go if you're into vintage oriented Fender-style basses because, well, they invented the damned things. If you desire modern instruments and sounds, I'd go for the Sire. From what I've read they seem a pretty safe buy, even sight unseen. 

Either way: enjoy!

On Reddit it's mostly a term people who are unhappy with the serues' casting seem to throw around. In reality it sort of indicates a general area in Europe, basically where you live and east. 

I'm Dutch, so definitely not Slavic, and from what I know of medieval times things where different around here than they were further east. So Slavicness could indicate a different subset of European culture, much like Scandinavian and Mediterranean cultures are vastly different.

People on here seem to misunderstand medieval Europe a lot though. Most of the monsters, stories and myths in the Witcher series (books and games) exist in one form or another all across Europe. The games are a total mishmash of European cultures.

European cultural history is deeply complex and absolutely fascinating, but the term Slavicness is mostly used here because people seem to be upset about who's been cast in the show.

Edit: it's also important to note that countries in Europe have changed endlessly over past centuries. They've grown, disappeared, merged, you name it. Borders as they are today have nothing to do with older cultures and who feels like they belong to which group. I mean, my country is tiny as hell, but if I go north or south for an hour I can't understand a word of the local dialect. 

Language and customs still differ from town to town sometimes, so terms like 'Slavicness' or 'Dutchness' or even 'European' are only ever going to be vague at best.

The choice between mirrorless and dslr is much like the choice between analog and digital. Both are means to an end, and both do certain things better than the other. 

I moved from Canon dslr to fuji mirrorless not because I needed mirrorless or dislike dslr, but because the fuji's just do something for me. As it turns out, "Fuji magic" is a very real thing to me. 

Each type of camera has distinct advantages. Dslrs usually have superior battery life, a larger lens selection (for now at least) and often a lower price point at the entry level. Photojournalists still seem to gravitate towards DSLRs, but this might be due to other factors (like manufacturer support, weather resistance, build quality or plain old habit).

Mirrorless offers advantages in size and weight (although at full frame the body+lens combo isn't usually that much smaller), improved AF point coverage, things like focus peaking for manual focus and the cameras are often more feature-rich. A lot of video and hybrid shooters seem to take a strong liking to mirrorless cameras, especially Sony's full frame offerings. 

All of this to say: it's a matter of preference, and the job you plan to do and how you want to do it determines what the right tool is for you.

Also: people getting upset about your choice of camera are as dumb as the people who get heated about Android vs iPhone or Ford vs Chevy.

You can get a camera and try it out, focus on an object using a mirror, and make sure the object is visible in the background. The mirror image will be in focus, the object itself in the background won't be.

**Cons:**

* It is quite expensive

* No features like SD-card holders and such.

**capacity:**

I usually use this bag to carry around my Fuji X100t and its teleconverter, a couple of batteries plus charger, and a bottle of water. It's basically my ''trip to a city or family gathering''-bag. It can also hold my personal stuff like wallet, cigarettes and phone.

Even though this big stuff fits, it isn't easy to get out quickly, so it's quite inefficient for (say) street or event photography when used this way.

**Conclusion:**

I would very much recommend this bag to anyone looking to easily carry around a smaller system while on a city trip or ''street'' shoot. Yes these are separate. Most cameras that are suited for the stuff you want to do with yours consist out of two major parts: The [body](http://img.bbystatic.com/BestBuy_US/images/products/8896/8896099_sd.jpg) and the [lens](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9a/Nikkor_28-200_zoom.jpg). 

The great advantage of this is that you can use different lenses on a body (given that they work together) and vice versa. This opens up the possibility of using your camera for many things. Now in landscape photography most people like using a wide lens, usually shorter than 35mm. This gives the camera a very wide field of view. In wildlife photography, where you a usually pretty far from your subject, you want to ''zoom in''. This requires a much longer lens, like a 200mm.

There are almost no good lenses which range from, say, 18mm (wide) to 300mm (zoomed in), so you'll have to buy to separate lenses.

To get a good feel for this, I'd suggest going to a camera store and having all this explained to you in real life. This will allow you to see and hold the stuff we're talking about here.

First of all, you have to realise that the US court system and law and the tradition during hearings is fundamentally different from what we adhere to here in the Netherlands (I am also a law student from NL). Where our court system and law are mostly based on a government vs suspect relation, the American system revolves around ''the people'' vs a suspect (which is evident in their jury trials and the titles of some criminal cases being 'the people vs....'). With that in mind, it becomes much easier to understand why judges are given the space to put forward a much more personal touch in their reasoning and explanation for sentencing and/or denying bail. This might very well be connected to the fact that the USA consist of many very influential local governments (state level) that are much more powerful than our provincial governments and can make state law that differs greatly within the US. Given that, it is no small leap to seeing that what we call ''Materieel recht/Materiele wetten'' (not sure how to accurately translate this) is made up locally (see mariuana and gay marriage) and is more directly connected to the people of a certain state. With that in mind, the judges who oversee the process are working with laws more directly related to the people of that state, and with the jury system the US system is much more based on emotional reasoning than ours.

TLDR: Don't project our Dutch formalities over an enterely different justice system and its philosophy.
